title: Abstract Group-Theoretic Product Formula: Unique Involution
description: In any finite commutative group with a unique non-trivial involution τ (τ² = 1, τ ≠ 1), the product of all elements equals τ. Every even-order cyclic group has exactly one such involution (the half-generator g^(|G|/2)), and odd-order groups have product 1. This provides the abstract group-theoretic core of the Gauss–Wilson theorem.

overview.historicalContext:
The classical argument behind Wilson's theorem and Gauss's generalization is an elegant group-theoretic observation: in a finite abelian group, elements pair with their inverses, and the product reduces to the self-inverse elements (those with x² = 1). The *abstract* form of this argument — that if there is a *unique* non-trivial involution τ, then ∏G = τ — distills the essence of the Gauss–Wilson theorem at the group-theoretic level, independent of modular arithmetic.

This perspective was implicit in Gauss's *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801) and made explicit in later treatments of group theory. For cyclic groups of even order, the unique involution is the half-generator g^(|G|/2), which corresponds to −1 in the concrete case (ℤ/nℤ)×.
overview.problemStatement:
For a finite commutative group G:
1. If τ ≠ 1 is the *unique* element satisfying τ² = 1, then ∏G = τ.
2. Every finite cyclic group of even order has exactly one such τ (namely g^(|G|/2) for any generator g).
3. Odd-order groups satisfy ∏G = 1.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Step 1** (Involution pairing): Apply `Finset.prod_involution` with σ = x⁻¹ to show ∏G = ∏{x | x²=1}. Elements not equal to their inverse pair up and cancel.

**Step 2** (Cardinality bound): In a cyclic group, `IsCyclic.card_pow_eq_one_le` gives |{x | x²=1}| ≤ 2.

**Step 3** (Unique involution → product): If {x | x²=1} = {1, τ}, then ∏{x | x²=1} = 1 · τ = τ via `Finset.prod_pair`.

**Step 4** (Even cyclic → unique involution): Generator g with orderOf(g) = |G|. Set τ = g^(|G|/2). Then τ² = g^|G| = 1 and τ ≠ 1 (else orderOf(g) | |G|/2, contradicting |G| = 2k). The cardinality squeeze {1,τ} ⊆ {x | x²=1} with |{x | x²=1}| ≤ 2 gives equality.

**Step 5** (Odd order → trivial): orderOf(x) | gcd(2, |G|) = 1, so x = 1 for all x with x² = 1. Thus {x | x²=1} = {1} and ∏G = 1.
keyInsights: The involution pairing ∏G = ∏{x | x²=1} is the universal reduction, valid for any finite abelian group
The cyclic group's polynomial degree bound (|solutions to x²=1| ≤ 2) provides the key constraint
A generator argument with g^(|G|/2) explicitly constructs the unique involution in even-order cyclic groups
The odd-order case follows from gcd(orderOf(x), 2) dividing gcd(|G|, 2) = 1
This file provides the abstract foundation that WilsonsTheoremOQ02 instantiates for (ℤ/nℤ)×
prerequisites: Finite abelian groups: Finset.prod_involution, product over filter

sections.title: Imports and Overview
sections.summary: Imports Mathlib.GroupTheory.SpecificGroups.Cyclic and Mathlib.Tactic. The docstring describes the main theorem (∏G = τ for unique involution τ), the cyclic corollary, and the three-step proof strategy: involution pairing, cardinality bound, generator argument.

sections.title: Part 1: Involution Pairing Lemma
sections.summary: Proves prod_eq_prod_involutions: in any finite abelian group, ∏G = ∏{x | x²=1}. Uses Finset.prod_involution with σ(x) = x⁻¹ to show non-self-inverse elements pair up and contribute product 1.

sections.title: Part 2: Cardinality Bound for Cyclic Groups
sections.summary: Proves card_sq_eq_one_le_two_cyclic: in any finite cyclic group, |{x | x²=1}| ≤ 2. Single-line proof via IsCyclic.card_pow_eq_one_le applied with n=2 (the polynomial degree bound for cyclic groups).

sections.title: Part 3: Abstract Product Formula
sections.summary: Proves prod_univ_of_unique_involution: if τ is the unique non-trivial involution, then ∏G = τ. Combines involution pairing with the identification {x | x²=1} = {1, τ}, then uses Finset.prod_pair to compute 1·τ = τ.

sections.title: Part 4: Unique Involution in Even Cyclic Groups
sections.summary: Proves IsCyclic.exists_unique_involution_of_even: every even-order cyclic group has a unique non-trivial involution g^(|G|/2). Constructs it explicitly via a generator argument and applies a cardinality squeeze to establish uniqueness.

sections.title: Part 5: Combined Cyclic Group Product Formula
sections.summary: Proves prod_cyclic_even_group: in any even-order cyclic group, ∃τ with τ≠1, τ²=1, and ∏G=τ. Composes Parts 3 and 4 in three lines. This is the abstract group-theoretic form of the Gauss–Wilson theorem.

sections.title: Part 6: Odd-Order Case
sections.summary: Proves prod_univ_odd_order: in a finite group of odd order, ∏G = 1. Shows x²=1 forces x=1 (since orderOf(x) ∣ gcd(2,|G|) = 1), so {x | x²=1} = {1} and the product is trivial.

crossReferences.title: Gauss's Generalization of Wilson's Theorem

crossReferences.title: Gauss-Wilson Theorem: Product of Units and Cyclic Groups
crossReferences.relationship: Sibling proof instantiating the abstract result for (ℤ/nℤ)×: the product of all units equals -1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)× is cyclic (equivalently, n is 1, 2, 4, p^k, or 2p^k for odd prime p).

crossReferences.title: Wilson's Theorem
crossReferences.relationship: Classical root: (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) iff p is prime. The unique involution in (ℤ/pℤ)× is -1, and Wilson's theorem is the special case where (ℤ/pℤ)× = ℤ/(p-1)ℤ is cyclic of even order p-1.

conclusion.summary: Proved the abstract group-theoretic product formula: in a finite abelian group, the product of all elements equals the unique non-trivial involution (when one exists uniquely). Even-order cyclic groups always have such a unique involution. Odd-order groups have trivial product. 6 theorems, 0 axioms, 235 lines, fully machine-verified.
conclusion.implications: This provides a self-contained abstract foundation for the Gauss–Wilson theorem. The concrete version (product of (ℤ/nℤ)× equals −1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)× is cyclic) follows by instantiating this abstract result. The key insight is that cyclicity (and only cyclicity among even-order finite abelian groups) guarantees uniqueness of the involution. For non-cyclic groups, multiple involutions force the product to be 1.
openQuestions: Generalize to non-abelian groups: when does ∏G = e for a finite group G?
Direct instantiation: apply prod_cyclic_even_group to (ZMod n)ˣ to give an alternative proof of Gauss–Wilson bypassing the Klein-four argument
